name: Self-tanning drops

lead: Self-tanning drops are concentrated DHA drops added to a regular moisturizer, body lotion or face cream so that the user can control how deep the tan develops.
They are popular for face tanning, where users want a gradual, customizable color without a separate product.

paras: Like all sunless tanners, DHA reacts with amino acids in the surface skin to create brown pigments, and the concentration in the mix sets the depth, with more drops giving a darker result. The effect is cosmetic and does not stimulate melanin or protect from UV.

Mixing errors can give uneven color, and drops can be too strong on the face. DHA has a good safety record on skin, but reviews call for more data on inhalation, and it should be kept away from lips, eyes and mucous membranes. It provides no sun protection, so sunscreen remains necessary.

lead: Self-tanning drops are concentrated dihydroxyacetone (DHA) preparations that users mix into a moisturizer, lotion or face cream, so that the number of drops determines how deep the resulting colour is. They are especially discussed for face tanning, where a gradual, adjustable colour is wanted. [1]

As with other sunless tanners, DHA reacts with amino acids in the outer dead layer of skin to produce brown pigments, a cosmetic effect that does not stimulate melanin or provide UV protection. [1][2][3]

A 2026 systematic review of 16 studies and a 2023 safety review describe DHA as having a generally favourable topical safety profile, minimal photoprotection that is insufficient to replace sunscreen, and remaining questions about inhalation and effects on cells in vitro. A 2024 survey of 44 popular self-tanning products found that contact allergens such as fragrances and propylene glycol were common ingredients. [2][4][5]
infobox: Cosmetic; DHA approved for external use only

paras: Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes drops as letting users customize tan intensity by adding more or fewer drops to a base product, producing a buildable colour. The same source gives DHA concentrations in sunless tanners of roughly 1 to 15 percent and colour lasting several days. [1]

DHA is a simple sugar that darkens the stratum corneum through a Maillard-type reaction with amino acids. Because it acts on surface cells, colour fades as these cells exfoliate. [1][6] The pigmentation response to UV light, driven by melanocyte signalling through MC1R and MITF, is a separate biological pathway not engaged by DHA.
No clinical studies of drop formulations specifically were found. Studies of DHA generally include the following.

A 2026 systematic review in the Journal of Cutaneous Medicine and Surgery included 16 studies in humans and animal models. It reported that mouse data suggest minimal photoprotection insufficient to replace sunscreen and possible delay of UV-linked tumour development, that people with erythropoietic protoporphyria and vitiligo may benefit from DHA, and that no link had been established between DHA and clinically relevant vitamin deficiency or contact dermatitis, while concerns remain about cutaneous effects. [2]

In a Thai study, 88.9 percent of 20 vitiligo patients reported moderate to marked satisfaction with 6 percent DHA cream as camouflage on exposed areas; a separate part of the study found higher DHA concentrations were needed to match darker skin. The study was small and partly retrospective. [7]

A cross-sectional review of 44 self-tanning products from 17 brands found an average of 11.86 contact allergens per product, most commonly propylene glycol, linalool, polysorbate, d-limonene, benzyl alcohol, tocopherol and fragrances. [5]

The FDA regulates sunless tanners as cosmetics, permits DHA for external use only and advises avoiding ingestion, inhalation and contact with mucous membranes. [4][6] Reviews describe irritant and allergic contact dermatitis as reported reactions. [4] DHA does not offer meaningful UV protection, so sunscreen is still recommended by dermatology reviews. [2][4]
Drops are used in appearance communities for face tanning and for adjusting colour depth in a routine. Application tools such as tanning mitts are used with other sunless tanners.
